lesson.title: Current: Charge on the Move
lesson.summary: This section defines electric current as the rate at which charge flows past a point, introduces the ampere as its unit, and explains the mechanism and direction convention behind it.
lesson.body:
You already know that electric charge is a property of matter that can push and pull on other charges, and that it comes in discrete positive and negative amounts. Current is what happens when that charge doesn't just sit still but actually moves through a material. Specifically, current is the rate at which charge passes a given point in a conductor: how much charge goes by per unit of time. If you imagine standing at one spot on a wire and counting the total charge that streams past you each second, that count is the current.

This gives current a precise numerical meaning. If an amount of charge Q passes a point in a time t, the current I is Q divided by t. The unit is the ampere, named after André-Marie Ampère, and one ampere means one coulomb of charge passing a point every second. So if 6 coulombs of charge flow through a wire in 3 seconds, the current is 6 divided by 3, or 2 amperes. If instead only 0.5 coulombs pass in that same 3 seconds, the current is much smaller, about 0.17 amperes. Notice that current is a rate, not a quantity of charge itself ,  a small current sustained for a long time can move just as much total charge as a large current for a short burst. A current of 2 amperes flowing for 10 seconds moves 20 coulombs of charge, since charge equals current multiplied by time.

Why does charge actually move through a conductor in the first place? In a conductor like copper wire, many electrons are only loosely bound to their atoms and are free to wander. Left alone, they jostle around randomly with no net motion in any direction, so no current exists even though charge is technically present everywhere. Current appears when something establishes an electric field along the conductor ,  typically a battery or other source of electrical energy ,  which exerts a consistent force on those free electrons. That force biases their random motion into a net drift in one direction, and it's this organized, directional flow of charge that we call current. The field itself is set up almost instantly throughout the wire, which is why a lamp switches on effectively right away even though the individual charges inside the wire are actually moving quite slowly.

One historical quirk you'll run into constantly is the direction convention for current. Long before anyone knew that electrons carry negative charge and are the actual moving particles in metal wires, physicists defined current as flowing from positive to negative terminals. That convention, called conventional current, stuck even after electrons were discovered moving the opposite way. So in a typical circuit, conventional current is described as flowing out of a battery's positive terminal, through the external components, and back into the negative terminal ,  while the electrons doing the physical moving are actually drifting in the reverse direction. This isn't a contradiction, just a labeling choice: current direction refers to the direction positive charge would move, whether or not positive charge is the thing actually in motion. Keeping this convention straight now will save you confusion later, once you start tracking current through more complex circuit diagrams.
